rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-6 <U+2013> own field evaluations of basin irrigation events at Pingluo (flumes, advance/recession, infiltrometer; Tables 3, 6, 7) and own runs of SRFR/SIRMOD and ISAREG. Q2: Section 6.2, Tables 11-12 and Conclusions <U+2013> ISAREG (FAO56 ETc, Kc, Ky, Ayers-Westcot salinity equations, Eqs. 3-9) used interactively with SRFR to search improved schedules for wheat, maize and intercrop, giving water savings of 30, 28 and 21% on non-saline soil with zero percolation, and 22, 15, 8% on saline soils while applying a ~8% leaching fraction; model outputs for present conditions were compared with field evaluations (Section 5.2 states computed percolation values are similar to those observed; Fig. 4 shows SRFR simulated vs observed advance/recession). Q4: Tables 7, 8, 11, 12 and Fig. 7 <U+2013> percolation, capillary rise, leaching depths and water-table depth are measured (Table 7) and modelled as the pathway by which scheduling saves water and controls salinity. Q5: Tables 8, 11, 12 <U+2013> results reported separately for three crops (wheat, maize, wheat-maize intercrop) and for three soil salinity conditions (non-saline, ECe 3 and ECe 11 dS/m), plus three infiltration soil types (Table 5). Q7: end of Section 6.2 <U+2013> savings achievable only under condition that upstream diversions are reduced so drainage functions, the drainage system is upgraded to lower the water table, precision zero leveling and higher inflow rates are adopted, and delivery scheduling is adapted; Conclusions restate water-table control as a pre-condition. Q8: Section 4.2 <U+2013> salt dynamics would require a mechanistic model, the ISAREG salinity subroutine only approximates effects on soil water availability and yield, and Eqs. 6-9 are valid only for RYL below 50%; Section 5.2 <U+2013> despite accuracy of the parametric functions some uncertainty remains in the water balance results.
rows.notes: The improved schedules and their water-saving/salinity-control outcomes are simulation scenarios (not observed); Q2 rated yes because the models were parameterised and checked against the study's own field evaluations of present conditions and the claim itself is that the study is an example of model-supported schedule search. Q3 no: the improved-schedule result rests on simulation alone, field evaluations only characterise present performance. Q5 yes is moderately held: all sites are in one district (Pingluo), but distinct crops and soil salinity classes are evaluated separately. Q6 no: results are for individual basins (e.g. B1); district-scale assessment is deferred to Gon<U+00E7>alves et al. (2007). Q9 no: ranges in Table 7 and SD in Table 3 concern present performance and field geometry, not dispersion or propagated uncertainty of the simulated savings; inflow-rate variations are scenarios.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study combines field evaluation of farmer basin irrigation with SRFR/SIRMOD and ISAREG simulations (FAO56 methodology with salinity corrections) to derive improved schedules in the Huinong Irrigation District.
